title: The Business Case For Learning And Development
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez makes the case that learning and development pays for itself once it is seen as a diagnostic and cost-saving tool rather than a discretionary expense. She argues that breakdowns in onboarding, handoffs and manager practice are learning failures that surface as delays, rework and turnover, so paying attention to where people struggle shows where the organization is leaking money. She names the costs of leaving learning to chance, shadow learning, distrust, firefighting and reputational risk, and offers two illustrative case studies of rework and manager turnover reduced by targeted L&D. She also rebuts the myth that small teams can wait, since a 15-person group has no slack to absorb weak onboarding. Her reframe is to ask where the organization is losing unnecessarily and how L&D can help.
points: Treating L&D as the diagnostic rather than the solution lets leaders see exactly where unclear standards are costing time, money and momentum.
Shadow learning from colleagues is adaptive but uneven, and it can send people off-script without anyone having told them the script.
Hidden costs of no clear standards include distrust, managers firefighting preventable problems, and reputational damage when quality varies by person.
Her illustrative cases tie learning to numbers, such as a $20K manager program set against over $200K to replace three departing employees.
Small organizations feel the lack of learning faster because there is little slack, and large ones pay the same cost through repetition.
quotes: I find one of the most frustrating things about L&D is that it’s often treated as the solution rather than the diagnostic. What I mean by this is that people see it as something we use to respond to an issue versus something we use to identify the issue.

The problem here has less to do with people’s fickleness around deadlines and more to do with the fact that the organization never clearly defined the handoff process. This is a perfect example of not only a learning breakdown, but the costs that can arise from it. Standards were never documented, expectations were never reinforced, and now the cost is showing up as delays, rework, and frustration.

Shadow learning is hardly malicious; it’s actually quite adaptive. People are trying to do good work with incomplete information. But when learning only happens in the “shadows,” without any kind of structure around it, it can be uneven, erroneous, and a source of major problems down the line.

If two people do the same task differently and both get praised, how does the company define “good?” And how can it be replicated? If one manager gives feedback one way and another gives it differently, how are people supposed to know what’s expected?

Six months later, manager-related complaints to HR decreased by 50%, and employee engagement scores around manager support and satisfaction increased by 25%. The cost of replacing those three employees was over $200K, whereas the program cost was $20K.

In a 15-person organization, there’s often very little slack. When one person struggles, the impact can be felt almost immediately. When onboarding is weak—or altogether lacking—everyone can feel the consequences.
